lawyer:
Sk Razzaque Ali with Munshi Ahsan Kabir, Advocates — For the Petitioner. 
Md Abdul Jabbar, Advocate — For the Opposite Party No. l.
parties:
Ali Akbar Khan ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Gurudas Mondal and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. The petitioner as plaintiff brought Title suit No. 270 of 1981 in the 2nd Court of Munsif at Khulna for declaration of title to the suit land. The suit was subsequently transferred to the court of Assistant Judge Dumuria and renumbered as Title suit No. 493 of 1983. The plaint case is that, the suit land measuring 1.21 acres originally belonged to one Shukchand Mondal who had 8 annas share as recorded in SA khatian No. 48, and 3 annas 4 gandas share in SA Khatian No. 2 of the mouza concerned. Sheikh Chand Mondal died leaving 5 sons namely, Jotin Mondal, Krishna Pada Mondal, Shahittya Mondal, Santosh Kumar Monda land Aditya Kumar Mondal, the defendants Nos. 16-20. While the said defendants were in possession of the land left by their father ''Shuk Chand Mondal, the two sons, defendants Nos. 16 and 17, transferred by registered kabala dated 24-1-74 land measuring .63 decimals of SA Khatian No. 48 and 6 decimal of SA khatian No. 2 to the plaintiff and inducted him into the possession of the land. The defendant No. 18 Shahittya Mondal, another son of Shukhand Mondal, transferred 32 decimal of land comprising SA Khatians Nos. 48 and 20 decimal of land comprising SA Khatian No. 2 by registered kabala dated 30-1-76 to the plaintiff and put the plaintiff in possession of the land. Thus the plaintiff acquired right, title, interest and possession in the land measuring 1.21 acres, and mutated his name in the Revenue Record and has been enjoying the land on payment of rent to the Government. While the plaintiff was in possession of his purchased land the defendant No. 1 filed an application under section 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to review the order of mutation made in favour of the plaintiff in Miscellaneous case No. 40/ 70-80. Having received the notice of the Miscellaneous case the plaintiff came to learn that the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 in collusion with the defendant No. 1 created a kabala dated 10-11-73 in favour of one Samad and Alauddin. On the date of execution and registration of the kabala dated 10-11-73 Shukchand Mondal was alive and he died on 18-12-83. According to the plaintiff, the kabala dated 10-11-73 is a product of fraud and it was made without any consideration and the recipients of the kabala did never enter into possession of the land and the kabala was not acted upon. Further assertion of the plaintiff is that, he came to know that Samad and Alauddin also created another registered kabala on 14-2-75 in favour of one Bhaggyadhar who never entered into possession of the land demised in the Kabala. Defendant No. 1 in collusion with Bhaggyadhor got another kabala registered 15-9-79 by Bhaggyadhar in his favour and the defendant No. 1 also never entered into possession of the land. All these transactions were mere paper truncations. It also transpired subsequently that the defendant Nos. 2-11 obtained some fraudulent and collusive documents which were also not acted upon. The plaintiff further asserted that in Miscellaneous the mutation in favour of the plaintiff was partially cancelled and encouraged by such cancellation the defendants denied the title of the plaintiff in the suit land on 28-8-81 and hence the suit. The plaintiff pleaded that he is a bonafide purchaser for value without knowledge of the transfer by kabala dated 10-11-73 and the subsequent transfer by various kabalas in favour of the defendant No. 1 by amendment petition the exact share of the plaintiff in the khatian was specified and in schedule No. 1 it has been mentioned that the plaintiff''s share in SA Khatian No. 48 is 4 annas and in schedule No. 2 the share of the plaintiff is 17 gandas. 

 4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations as made in the plaint. The defendant''s case is that Shuk Chand died leaving defendant Nos. 16-20 as his heirs, while the said defendants were in possession of the land left by their father the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 sold 1.00 acre of land to Abdus Samad and Alauddin Biswas by registered kabala dated 10-11-73 and the said purchasers entered into possession of 0.64 acres of land and thereafter they transferred the said land to Bhaggyadhar and Ful Chand by registered kabala dated 14-2-75 who in turn sold the land to the defendant No. 1 by registered kabala dated 15-9-79. The defendant Nos. 10-20 sold 9.66 acres of land to one Atul Krishna Mondal by registered kabala dated 4-7-74 and put the purchaser in possession. Subsequently the defendants Nos. 18-20 took back land from Atul Krishna by kabala dated 15-5-78 and thereafter sold that same to the defendant Nos.  2-11 and one Golam Rahman by registered kabala on the same date i.e. on 15-5-78. After the death of Golam Rahman the defendant Nos.  2-11 as his heirs became the owners of the said land. Defendant Nos. 16 and 17 also sold 0.25 acres of land to Golam Rahman on 20-5-78. Thus Golam Rahman acquired 0.66 acres of land in SA khatian No. 48 and 0.25 acres land in SA Khatian No. 2 and the defendant No. 2-11 are in possession of the land and thereafter the defendant Nos. 2-11 sold the said land to the defendant No. 1 by various kabalas. The defendant thus became the owner of the land and he has been in peaceful possession of the land being a co-sharer in both the khatians. Specific claim of the defendant No. 1 is that by purchase as well as by way of inheritance he acquired title and possession in 2.97 acres of land out of 3.29 acres of SA Khatian No. 48 and 2.84 acres out of 4.94 acres of land of SA Khatian No. 2 and accordingly, he has been in possession of the said land and paying rent to the Government. The plaintiff has no manner of possession in the suit land and the documents of title of the plaintiff are fabricated. 

 6. Admittedly the suit land belonged to Shuk Chand Mondal, father of the defendant Nos. 16-20. The claim of the plaintiff is that the defendants Nos. 16 and 17 transferred 63 decimal of land comprising khatian No. 48 and 6 decimal of land comprising khatian No. 2 to the plaintiff by registered sale deed dated 24-1-76. The plaintiff''s further claim is that the defendant No. 18 Satya Mondal transferred 22 decimals of land of khatian No. 48 and 20 decimals from khatian No. 2 by deed dated 30-1-76 to the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 claims that defendants Nos. 16 and 17 transferred 1.00 acre of land to Samad and Alauddin by kabala dated 10-11-73 and the said purchasers got possession upon 64 decimal of land which was transferred to Bhaggyadhar and Fulchand. The plaintiff''s specific allegation in the plaint is that the defendant No. 1 had always been the main man and the mastermind in creating all those kabalas including the kabala dated 10-11-73. The defendant No. 1 is admittedly the nephew of Mondal i.e. his brother''s son. The plaintiffs claim is that the defendants Nos. 16 and 17 had no legal right and legitimate authority to transfer the land of the khatian to Biswas and Alauddin by kabala dated 10-11-73 because Mondal, the father of defendants Nos. 16 and 17, was then alive, and he died on 19-12-73 and this fact was very much know to the defendant No. 1 and also Samad and Alauddin. 

 8. The learned subordinate Judge appears to have misread the evidence, particularly the documentary evidence Ext, 5 the death certificate of Shukchand Mondal and wrongly held that there is no clear and direct proof that Shukchand was alive at the time of sale of the land measuring 1.00 acre by the defendants Nos. 16 and 17 by deed dated 10-11-73. The death certificate having not been denied by the defendant No. 1, nor there is any oral testimony from the side of the defendant that at the time of transfer by defendant Nos. 16 and 17 in favour of Abdus Samad and Alauddin, Shukchand was alive, the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is held to be perverse not being supported by any evidence. It appears from the judgment of the Appellate Court that the finding of possession arrived at by the trial Court has not been reversed referring to the evidence and therefore the trial Court''s finding that the plaintiffs is in possession is maintained. No reason has been assigned by the learned Subordinate judge, how the title passed toSamad and Alauddin by kabala dated 10-11-73 executed and registered by defendant Nos. 16 and 17 when their father Shukhand Mondal was alive. No valid reason has been assigned how the title of Jatian and Krishnapada was extinguished before their transfer to the plaintiff by deed dated 24-1-76. It is the specific case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff is a bonafide purchaser for consideration without notice of the existence of transfer made by his vendors and to that effect evidence was laid by the plaintiff. The purchase by kabala dated 10-11-73 by Samad and Alauddin, according to the plaintiff, is unauthorised under the provision of law in that the fact that Shukhand was alive was known to both the transferees and the transfer or of the said deed. Apparently there was no contest as to the quantum of land purchased by the plaintiff by the two deeds, but the learned Appellate Judge made out a new case about the proportionate share of the plaintiff in the suit khatian and wrongly held that the trial Court has given more land to the plaintiff than what the plaintiff is entitled to. 

 9. Next comes the question of maintainability of the suit as per provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Subordinate Judge having found that there are other co-sharers in the suit khatians who are also possessing the land the plaintiffs must have sought for a relief for partition and thus held that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 10. In order to confront this situation Mr Sk Razzak Ali, the learned advocate has submitted that the learned Appellate Court erroneously held that the suit is barred under the aforesaid provision of law. His contention is the plaintiff being in possession had sought for declaration of his title in the land i.e. the plaintiff is seeking a relief for his entitlement in the suit land which has been denied by the defendant. His further submission is that the plaintiff''s title in respect of his share namely, 4 annas 4 gondas in schedule 1 and 17 gandas in schedule 2 of which he is in possession may be declared and the plaintiff was not able to seek further than a mere declaration of title which he has committed. The possession of the plaintiff has been proved by evidence and that has been found by the trial Court. The finding of possession has not been reversed by the appellate Judge referring to the material evidence. He had further argued that even if it is found that the plaintiff is in joint possession of the land of the suit khatian, still the plaintiff is entitled to a declaration of his title to the extent of his share and in a case like this suit for pure declaration is maintainable. To find support he has placed reliance upon a decision in the case of Joy Narayan Sen Ukil vs Suchitra Debya reported in 1921 Calcutta Law Journal Vol.33 page 502. In the case under reference the plaintiff instituted a declaratory suit, and on the allegation that he was in joint possession of the one third share claimed by him, he did not seek consequential relief. The claim for declaratory relief was resisted on the grounds amongst others that it was barred by limitation and that even it was well founded, in fact, the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the plaintiff had omitted to claim further relief. The subordinate Judge found on the evidence that the plaintiff was in joint possession of his share and that the claim for declaratory relief was not barred by limitation but the subordinate Judge held, however, that the plaintiff might have claimed further relief by way of partition, and in this view he dismissed the suit. The plaintiff appealed against the decree and has assailed the reason assigned by the Court below for withholding the declaration justified by the facts found. It was held that where the plaintiff is in joint possession of immovable property, whether such possession be actual possession of his share of the whole, or actual possession of a part coupled with constructive possession of the remainder, he is entitled to maintain a suit for declaratory relief with a view to remove a cloud of his title created by the act of the defendant disputing his share. In a suit so framed, declaration of title is all that the plaintiff needs and he is consequently not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition. The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, forbids a suit for pure declaration without further relief; but it does not compel a plaintiff to sue for all the relief which could possibly be granted, or debar him from obtaining a relief which he wants unless at the same time he asks for a relief which he does not want. The expression further relief in the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, means relief in relation to the legal character or rights as to property which the plaintiff is entitled to and whose title to such character or right the defendant denied is interested in denying; it must also be relief appropriate to and necessarily consequential of the right or title asserted to. It has further been observed that one of the incidents of joint property is that it may be enjoyed jointly, another incident is that a joint character is liable to be terminated. If a co-owner is content to enjoy joint property as such, he should not be driven to seek for partition, merely because his co-owner chooses to dispute the extent of his share. The principle laid down in the case cited is in all fours applicable in the instant case. This view has been consistently followed in various decisions of the courts of the subcontinent including our Courts. When the plaintiff being in possession seeking for declaration he need not seek any further relief as contemplated under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 16. Mr Abdul Jabbar has contended that the suit land having not been specified and demarcated by boundary the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief in the form of declaration. To substantiate his contention he has cited a decision in the case of Tayebali vs Abdul Khaleque and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87. In the case the land was very much specified and demarcated as given in the schedule of the plaint but the possession of the plaintiff or his predecessor donor could not be proved. In the present case the plaintiff is claiming not only the quantum of land as described in the schedule but also the extent of share in the suit khatian and the plaintiff is in possession of his share claimed. In that view of the matter the cited case has no manner of application. 

 17. Mr Jabbar has further argued that for not having complied with the provision of Order 7 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure the plaintiff is not entitled to any declaratory decree in respect of an immovable property because the suit land is not specified with boundaries and other particulars. This plea was not taken by the defendant in the written statements nor any issue was framed to that effect nor any case was made out by adducing evidence and further that in this respect it has not been urged before the trial Court and the Appellate Court below that the suit land is unspecified and vague. It is contended for the first time before this Court that the provision of Order 7 rule 3 has not been complied with in claiming the land in the suit. The suit being one for declaration of tithe, no relief has been sought for confirmation of possession or recovery of khas possession. Mr Sk Razzak Ali has contend that in a declaratory decree no execution is necessary. Specification of the land by boundary is required or may be a legal requirement in case of execution of decree for recovery of khas possession or in a decree for confirmation of possession. The plaintiff needs only a declaration as to his entitlement over his share in the land. His contention in this regard appears to be sound and acceptable. but this point was not at all confounded by the plaintiff in the court below. In the 42 DLR''s case (Noor Mohammad Khan and others vs Government of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh and others; page 434) as has been cited by Mr Md Abdul Jabbar, maintainability of the suit was decided on the basis of the plaintiff''s possession and it was held that plaintiff having failed to prove his possession in the suit land simple suit for declaration of his title is barred. So far the specification according to Order 7 rule 3 is concerned the plaintiff has given in the schedule, name of the mouzas, Khatian numbers, plot numbers, the quantum of land as well as the specific share of the plaintiff. Although the boundary has not been given but the plaintiff will be able to manage his possession in his share according to his entitlement in the property. It is not the case that the other co-sharers are claiming that the plaintiff is possessing more land than his share. In view of the above facts and circumstances the provision as laid down under Order 7 rule 3 cannot strictly apply.
